title: Proteomic Analysis of the E6 Interactome in Response to Anisomelic Acid Treatment
projectDescription: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a well-known cause of cervical cancer, with the viral oncoprotein E6 playing a key role in carcinogenesis. We previously showed that anisomelic acid treatment reduces E6 protein levels in HPV-positive cancer cells. In this study, we used mass spectrometry-based proteomics to investigate how anisomelic acid affects the HPV16 E6 interactome in normal oral keratinocytes.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Co-immunoprecipitated samples were subjected to on-bead digestion protocol. Beads were digested with 5 µg/ml trypsin in 6 volumes of 2M urea, 25 mM ammonium bicarbonate (ABC) pH 7.5 at 27°C with shaking at 800 rpm for 30 minutes. The supernatant was collected, and beads were washed twice with 2.5 volumes of 2 M urea, 25 mM ABC, 1 mM DTT. All supernatants were pooled and digested overnight at room temperature. After digestion, peptides were alkylated for 30 minutes in the dark with IAA. Samples were then acidified with trifluoroacetic acid prior to desalting using a Sep-Pak C18 96-well plate (40 mg, Waters). Desalted peptides were dried, dissolved in 0.1% formic acid and 400 ng of each sample was used for LC-MS/MS analysis. The analysis was conducted using an EASY-nLC 12000 HPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a nano-electrospray ionization source. Samples were first loaded onto a trap column (100 µm internal diameter × 2 cm) and then separated on an analytical column (75 µm internal diameter × 15 cm), both packed in-house with ReproSil-Pur C18-AQ resin (3 µm, 120 Å, Dr. Maisch HPLC GmbH). The elution was was achieved using a 60-minute gradient at a constant flow of 300 nL/min: 8–21% solvent B over 28 min, 21–36% B over 22 min, 36–100% B over 5 min, followed by by a 5-minute wash at 100% B. Solvent B consisted of 80% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid in water. Full-scan MS spectra data were acquired at a resolution of 120,000 (m/z range 300–1750), with an AGC target of 700,000, and a maximum injection time of 50 ms. Precursor ions with charge states >+2 and intensities >25,000 were selected for fragmentation within a 2.5-second cycle. Fragmentation was performed by HCD using a normalized collision energy of 27%. MS/MS spectra were acquired in the Orbitrap at a resolution of 30,000, an AGC target of 50,000 and a maximum injection time of 75 ms. Dynamic exclusion was set to 35 seconds with a mass tolerance of 10 ppm.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw LC-MS/MS data were analyzed using either MaxQuant (version 2.0.1.0) or FragPipe (version 21.1) with MSFragger (version 4.0), IonQuant (version 1.10.12), and Philosopher (version 5.1.0). For MaxQuant searches, spectra were searched against a UniProt database containing HPV proteins (UP000009251; 9 entries) and the human proteome (UP000005640; 78,120 entries), downloaded on August 1, 2021. Methionine oxidation and N-terminal acetylation were set as variable modifications, and cysteine carbamidomethylation as a fixed modification. Trypsin digestion with a maximum of 2 missed cleavages was allowed. The mass tolerance was 20 ppm for the first search and 4.5 ppm for the main search. LFQ was enabled with a minimum ratio count of 2, using unique+razor peptides for quantification. A 1% FDR was applied at both peptide and protein levels. The "match between runs" option was enabled with a 2-minute matching window and a 20-minute alignment window. For FragPipe processing, spectra were searched against the UniProt human proteome (UP000005640; downloaded September 5, 2023, containing 40,912 entries with 50% generated reverse decoys). The default LFQ-MBR workflow was used with precursor and fragment mass tolerances of 20 ppm. Trypsin digestion allowing up to two missed cleavages was applied. Methionine oxidation was used as a variable modification, and cysteine carbamidomethylation as a fixed modification. Protein and peptide FDR were both set to 1%.
